title: Machine Learning I — How Machines Learn From Data

lessons.title: Examples in, rules out: the inversion of programming
paragraphs: In, in. Come on in and sit down. I am Professor Sana Rahal, and this is Machine Learning One, How Machines Learn From Data. This is our very first lesson together, and its title tells you almost the whole secret in five words. Examples in, rules out, the inversion of programming. Inversion is a plain word once we unpack it. It means a turning upside down, a flipping of the order you expected. In this lesson you will learn what ordinary programming does, what machine learning does instead, why that flip matters, and how to spot which approach fits which job. By the end you will be able to explain the difference to a friend in your own words, with no jargon left unpacked, and you will see why this one flip changed what computers can do for a small business, for a family, and for the world. My office door carries a little hand-written sign that says stuck is a place, not a person. If you feel stuck at any point in this lesson, that is fine. Stuck is just where we start. We draw the diagram first, and then we name the thing. That is how I teach, and that is how we will go today.

Let me draw the first diagram in words, slowly. Picture two boxes on a whiteboard. In the first box, on the left, I write the word rules. In the second box, in the middle, I write the word computer. An arrow goes from rules into the computer, and another arrow comes out of the computer on the right into a third box that says answers. That is ordinary programming. A person thinks hard, writes down exact rules, feeds those rules into the computer, and the computer follows the rules to produce answers. Now picture a second diagram underneath it. In the first box this time I write the word examples. In the middle box I still write computer, but I add underneath it the words learning program. An arrow goes from examples into that learning program, and the arrow coming out on the right does not go to answers this time. It goes to a box that says rules. That is machine learning. A person gathers many examples, feeds those examples into a learning program, and the program works out rules of its own. Same computer. Opposite direction. Rules in, answers out is the old way. Examples in, rules out is the new way. Hold onto that picture, because everything else in this whole class is just that picture getting more detailed.

Let me make the old way completely concrete, because you already know it from everyday life even if you have never written a line of code. Code is just instructions written in a language a computer can follow exactly. A program is a set of those instructions. Suppose you run a small shop and you want a simple program to work out a discount. You might tell the computer, in plain English first, if a customer spends more than one hundred dollars, take ten percent off, otherwise charge the full price. That is a rule. You thought of it. You decided the number one hundred and the number ten percent. The computer did not decide anything. It just obeys, quickly and without getting tired. Or suppose you want a program to add up a till at the end of the day. You tell it, take every sale, add them one by one, and print the total. Again, you supplied the method. The computer supplied the speed. For jobs like that, ordinary programming is perfect, because you already know the rule and the rule does not change. A calculator is the purest case. You press seven plus five, and deep inside, rules about addition turn your input into the answer twelve. Nobody needs the calculator to learn addition from examples. The rule for addition is known, exact, and settled. When the rule is known and exact, write the rule. That is lesson zero, and it never stops being true.

Now feel where the old way starts to strain. Suppose you want a program that looks at an email and decides whether it is junk mail or real mail. Try to write the rules yourself. You might start with, if the email says free money, mark it as junk. That catches some junk. Then the junk senders stop writing free money and start writing free m0ney with a zero instead of the letter o. So you add another rule. Then they change again. You add a rule about links, a rule about capital letters, a rule about certain senders, a rule about spelling mistakes. After a month you have five hundred rules, after a year you have five thousand, and the junk still slips through, because the other side keeps changing and because real mail sometimes looks a little bit like junk too. A note from your bank about a free service is real. A note from a stranger about free money is not. The difference is real, but it is fuzzy, and fuzzy differences are very hard to write as exact rules by hand. The same strain shows up with pictures. Write a rule for telling a cat from a dog in a photograph. Furry, four legs, tail — that describes both. Pointy ears — some dogs have those too. You can feel the pattern when you see a hundred cats and a hundred dogs, but turning that feeling into exact written rules defeats almost everyone. The pattern is in the examples, not in a rule you can state in advance. That gap, between a pattern you can recognise in examples and a rule you cannot write by hand, is exactly the gap machine learning was built to cross.

So here is the new way, step by step, with nothing hidden. First, you collect examples. An example is one case where you already know the answer. For the junk mail job, an example is one email together with its correct label, junk or not junk. Label is our second new word, and it just means the correct answer attached to an example. A pile of examples with their labels is called training data. Training is the word for the learning process itself, and training data is the pile the machine learns from. Second, you choose a kind of flexible pattern-finder, called a model. A model is a mathematical shape with adjustable settings inside it, a bit like a radio with many dials. At the start the dials are set almost at random, so the model is useless. Third, you show the model the examples one by one. For each example, the model makes a guess, you compare the guess with the true label, and you nudge the dials a tiny bit in the direction that would have made the guess better. We will spend whole lessons later on how that nudging works, so for now just hold the picture of dials being nudged, example after example. Fourth, after seeing many examples, sometimes thousands, sometimes millions, the dial settings settle into a pattern that works well on the examples. Those settled dial settings are, in effect, the rules the machine found. Nobody wrote them. They grew out of the examples. Fifth and last, you use the model on new cases it has never seen, and if it learned well, it guesses well there too. Examples in, rules out. That five-step story is the whole of machine learning in miniature, and every lesson in this class zooms into one part of it.

I want to slow down on the word rules, because it can mislead you if we are not careful. When I say the machine finds rules, I do not mean it writes sentences like if the email says free money, mark it as junk. Sometimes the rules it finds can be read almost like sentences, and later courses look at those cases. But usually the rules are numbers, dial settings, weights — we will meet that word properly in the next lessons — that work together in a way no human would read like a story. The rules are real, in the sense that they decide what the model does, but they live as numbers inside the model, not as English on a page. That is both the power and the price of the flip. The power is that the machine can capture patterns too fuzzy and too tangled for us to write down. The price is that we cannot always explain, in plain sentences, exactly why the model gave the answer it gave. We can test whether it works. We can measure how often it is right. But reading its mind is harder than reading a rule a person wrote. A good practitioner never forgets that trade. You gain reach, and you give up some transparency, and you manage that trade with honest testing, which is where this class will end, in lesson six, with the exam the model has never seen.

Let me give you a small worked example you can follow entirely in your head, with tiny numbers, because numbers make the flip vivid. Imagine you sell jam at a market stall, and you want to predict how many jars you will sell on a Saturday based on the weather. You have no rule for that. Nobody does. But you have your notebook from the last four Saturdays. Saturday one was sunny and you sold twenty jars. Saturday two was sunny and you sold twenty-two jars. Saturday three was rainy and you sold ten jars. Saturday four was rainy and you sold twelve jars. Those four lines in your notebook are training data. Each line is an example. The weather is the input, what you are shown, and the number of jars is the label, the correct answer for that day. Now, what rule would a human eye find in those four lines? Sunny days average twenty-one jars, because twenty and twenty-two average to twenty-one. Rainy days average eleven jars, because ten and twelve average to eleven. So the rule the examples suggest is simple. If it is sunny, expect about twenty-one jars. If it is rainy, expect about eleven jars. Next Saturday the forecast says sunny, so you pack twenty-one jars, maybe a couple extra to be safe. Notice what just happened. You did not start with a rule about jam and weather handed down by an expert. You started with examples and the rule came out of them. You just did, by hand and in miniature, exactly what a learning program does at scale. The machine would do the same averaging in spirit, though with far more examples, far more inputs than just weather, and dials nudged by a careful procedure instead of by your eye. If the numbers had been messier, say sunny days selling eighteen, twenty-five, nineteen and thirty, your eye would still find roughly the middle, and so would the machine. Learning, at its heart, is finding the pattern that sits in the middle of messy examples. That is worth saying twice. Learning is finding the pattern that sits in the middle of messy examples.

Now let us test the flip on a second everyday job, a little bigger, still from a small business owner's real life. Imagine you run a small marketing service. Clients come to you because they want more customers. Every week, people fill in a form on your website. Some of those people become paying clients, and most do not. After a year you have records on, let us say, two hundred people who filled in the form. For each person you know a few facts, how they found you, how big their business is, whether they opened your follow-up email, and crucially, whether they became a client or not. That last fact is the label. Could you write exact rules by hand for who will become a client? You could try. People with bigger businesses, maybe. People who open the email, maybe. But the real pattern is a blend. Perhaps people from referrals who open the email and run a business with five to twenty staff become clients quite often, while people from a cold advert who never open anything almost never do, with dozens of shades in between. Writing that blend as exact hand rules is the junk mail problem all over again. But feeding the two hundred examples to a learning program is natural. The program nudges its dials until its guesses line up with what actually happened across those two hundred cases. Then, when a new person fills in the form next week, the model gives you a score, a sense of how likely this person is to become a client, and you spend your limited calling time on the most promising people first. You have not replaced your judgment. You have aimed it. That is a sentence I want you to keep for the whole course. A good model does not replace your judgment, it aims it. And notice, the model only knows what the examples taught it. If your two hundred records all came from one town, the model may misjudge people from a very different town. The examples set the limits of the rules. Garbage examples in, garbage rules out, is the old warning, and it is exactly right. The flip does not create wisdom from nothing. It extracts the pattern that is actually in the data you gave it, no more and no less.

Here is a third angle on the same flip, and it is the one that helps most people feel it in their bones. Think about how a child learns the word dog. Nobody hands a two-year-old a written definition with rules about ears and tails and then tests her on the definition. Instead, adults point. That is a dog. That is a dog too. That is a cat, not a dog. Example after example, with labels spoken aloud, and slowly the child builds an inner pattern that lets her point at a dog she has never seen before and say dog, correctly, with delight. She cannot state her rules. Ask her why that one is a dog and she will say because it just is. Her rules live in her, as tuned connections, not as sentences. Machine learning copies that human route on purpose. It learns the way children learn, from labelled examples, because for fuzzy patterns in a messy world, that route works where the definition route fails. And it fails the way children fail too. Show a child only tiny dogs and she may call a horse a big dog. Show a model only one narrow kind of example and it will make the matching mistake. The cure in both cases is the same, broader and better examples, honestly labelled. When you hear someone say the machine learned, this is the honest meaning underneath the phrase. Nobody programmed the answer. The pattern was grown from examples, the way a child's pattern grows from pointing and naming.

We should also be precise about what the flip is not, because loose talk causes real confusion. Machine learning is not magic, and the model does not understand the world the way you do. Your jam model does not know what rain is. It knows that in your notebook, the rainy lines carried smaller numbers. Machine learning is not the same as ordinary statistics disappearing, either. Averages, like our twenty-one and eleven, are part of its toolkit, not a rival to it. And machine learning is not always the right tool. If the rule is known and exact, write the rule. Adding up a till, working out tax at a fixed rate, checking whether a password matches the stored password — these want written rules, exact and auditable, and a learning model would only add fog. A professional chooses. Known rule, stable world, exact answer needed — write the program. Fuzzy pattern, plenty of examples, a good guess is valuable — teach the model. Some real systems mix both, written rules guarding the edges while a model handles the fuzzy middle. Knowing which half of the diagram you are in, rules in or examples in, is the first skill of this whole field, and you now have it.

Let me pause and do a guided think-it moment with you, the way we will in every lesson, because doing a small piece yourself fixes it in memory far better than hearing it twice. In your head, or on paper if you have paper, picture the two diagrams again. Top diagram, rules in, answers out. Bottom diagram, examples in, rules out. Now take three jobs and sort them. Job one, working out ten percent off a price over one hundred dollars. Job two, spotting junk mail. Job three, predicting jam sales from the weather using your notebook. Give each job a home. Take your time. I will wait a breath while you sort them. Here is how I sort them. Job one lives in the top diagram. The rule is known and exact, so we write it. Jobs two and three live in the bottom diagram. Their patterns are fuzzy, the examples exist, and a good guess is worth money and time, so we learn them. If you sorted them that way, you have understood the lesson's core. If one landed differently, ask yourself which question decided it. Was the rule already known and exact, or was the pattern hiding in examples? That single question is the sorting tool. Keep it in your pocket. Was the rule already known and exact, or was the pattern hiding in examples? You will use it in every lesson that follows, and honestly, in every sales pitch about artificial intelligence you will ever hear for the rest of your life.

One more worked pass, because I want the dials picture to be solid before lesson two builds on it. Imagine a model as a single dial and a single job, guessing jam sales on sunny days only. The dial is the model's current guess for a sunny day, one number. You start the dial at zero, a silly guess. First sunny example, you sold twenty jars. The guess of zero is too low by twenty, so you nudge the dial up, but only part of the way, say to ten. Second sunny example, you sold twenty-two jars. The guess of ten is too low by twelve, so you nudge up again, say to sixteen. Third sunny example, twenty jars again. The guess of sixteen is low by four, nudge to eighteen. You can feel the dial homing in, step by smaller step, toward the neighbourhood of twenty-one, the average we found earlier. That homing-in, done patiently over many examples, is training. The final dial position is the learned rule for sunny days, in the form of a number. Real models have thousands or millions of dials and a far cleverer nudging method, which lesson four will teach you under its proper name, gradient descent. But the soul of it is already here in this little dial story. Guess, compare with the truth, nudge, repeat. Guess, compare, nudge, repeat. If you remember nothing else from today, remember those four beats, because they beat underneath every machine learning system ever built, from a jam stall notebook to the largest systems on earth.

Let me also name the people in this story, because in real work these roles matter. The person who collects and labels the examples is doing data work, and sloppy labels poison everything downstream. The person who chooses the model shape and runs the training is doing modelling work. The person who will use the model's guesses, like you deciding whom to call first, is the decision maker, and the model serves that person's decision, not the other way round. In a small business, one person may wear all three hats in a single afternoon. In a hospital or a bank, whole teams split the hats. Either way, the flip stays the same at the centre. Somewhere, examples went in, and rules came out, and a decision got better aimed because of it. When a vendor tells you their system uses artificial intelligence, the grown-up follow-up questions are now yours to ask. What examples did it learn from? How many, and how honestly labelled? How do you test it on cases it has never seen? A vendor who can answer those clearly has a real system. A vendor who cannot is selling fog. This class will give you, lesson by lesson, the knowledge to tell the difference for yourself.

Before we recap, let me answer the three questions every beginner asks at this point, because you may be asking them quietly right now. First question, does the machine think up its rules from nothing, like an inventor? No, and this matters. The person still chooses the shape of the model, chooses which examples to collect, chooses what counts as the label, and chooses how success will be measured. The machine searches inside the space the person built. It is a powerful search, and it finds patterns no person spotted, but it searches where it was pointed. Human judgment frames the job at both ends, before training and after it. Second question, how many examples does learning need? It depends on how fuzzy the pattern is and how much the examples vary. Our jam rule settled with four examples because the pattern was simple, one input, weather, and two clear groups. Junk mail needs tens of thousands of examples because senders vary endlessly and real mail varies too. A useful rule of thumb is this, the fuzzier the pattern and the more ways the world can vary, the more examples you need before you should trust the rules that come out. Third question, can the learned rules ever beat the person who collected the examples? At the narrow job they were trained on, yes, often, and that is not spooky. You can recognise thousands of faces yet be unable to write the rule for even one. A model trained on enough labelled faces can sort new faces more reliably than you can, while knowing nothing about birthdays, jokes, or friendship. Narrow skill grown from examples can exceed the teacher on that narrow skill, while general understanding stays entirely with the person. Holding both halves of that sentence at once, impressed by the narrow skill and clear-eyed about the missing understanding, is the mature attitude this whole class is trying to build in you.

One last story, and it is a true shape of story even though the stall is mine, about the cost of choosing the wrong side of the flip. A shopkeeper I imagine, let us call her Ana, runs a bakery and wants to know which mornings will be busy so she can bake the right amount and waste less. Ana first tries the rules route. She writes rules with her nephew. Rainy mornings are quiet, except when they are not, because the school run still happens. Sunny Fridays are busy, except in the holidays. She ends the month with a notebook full of exceptions, each rule patched with an unless, and the waste barely moves. Then Ana tries the examples route. For sixty mornings she simply records what happened. The day, the weather, whether school was in, whether the roadworks were active, and the label, how many loaves she sold by ten o'clock. Sixty honest examples. The pattern that comes out is one she could feel but never state. Roadworks plus school plus rain is her busiest combination, because drivers stuck in traffic buy coffee and bread while they wait. No hand-written rule of hers had ever joined those three facts together. Her waste falls, not to zero, because the world keeps some randomness, but enough to matter every single week. Ana did not become a programmer. She became a good collector of examples, and she asked the grown-up questions about testing before she trusted the scores. That is the realistic promise of this field for a small business. Not robots, not magic, just patterns you already half know, made solid by examples you already half have, once you flip which side of the diagram you start from.

Time to recap, in order, the way we will always recap. First, ordinary programming is rules in, answers out. A person writes exact rules, and the computer follows them. Second, machine learning flips that order. It is examples in, rules out. A learning program studies labelled examples and finds its own rules, held as dial settings inside a model. Third, an example is one case with a known answer, that known answer is its label, and the pile of examples is the training data. Fourth, training follows four beats, guess, compare with the truth, nudge the dials, repeat, until the guesses line up with the examples. Fifth, the flip wins where patterns are fuzzy and examples are plentiful, like junk mail, pictures, and likely clients, and it loses where rules are known and exact, like addition, discounts, and tax, where you should simply write the rule. Sixth, the learned rules are only as good as the examples, because the pattern in the data is all the machine can extract. Examples in, rules out, but honest examples, or the rules will mislead you with a straight face.

That brings us to the close of lesson one. You have done real work today. You can draw both diagrams, sort jobs between them, and tell the jam stall story from notebook to rule. In our next lesson, Features and labels, what the machine is shown, we will open up the example itself and look inside it. We will ask, what exactly does the machine see when it looks at one example, which parts are the clues and which part is the answer, and how choosing the clues well or badly decides whether learning succeeds before it even starts. For now, the questions on this lesson are waiting for you, and they are built only from what I taught you here. The full text of this lesson stays open beside the questions, and going back to read a passage again is learning, not cheating, so use it freely. Work through them at your own pace, easy ones first, and remember the sign on my door. Stuck is a place, not a person. You were stuck on this flip an hour ago, in a manner of speaking, and now you are not. That is the whole game. I will see you in lesson two.

lessons.title: Features and labels: what the machine is shown
paragraphs: Welcome back. In, in, take your seat. I am Professor Sana Rahal, and this is Machine Learning One, lesson two, Features and labels, what the machine is shown. Last time we flipped programming on its head. Examples in, rules out. Today we open up one example and look inside it, because an example is not one solid lump. It has parts, and the parts have different jobs. Some parts are the clues the machine is shown. Some part is the answer we want it to learn to predict. If you mix those jobs up, learning fails before it starts, quietly and expensively. If you get them right, even a simple model can do honest, useful work. By the end of this lesson you will know what a feature is, what a label is, how to choose features with care, how to spot a cheating feature that secretly contains the answer, and how to turn messy real life, like words, categories and missing entries, into numbers a machine can actually use. We draw the diagram before we name the thing, as always, so let us draw.

Picture one example as a row in a table, like a row in a notebook or a spreadsheet. The row has several columns, and then one special column at the end, set apart. The columns before the special one are the features. A feature is one measurable clue about the case, one fact the machine is allowed to look at when it makes its guess. The special column at the end is the label. The label is the correct answer for that row, the thing we want the machine to learn to predict for new rows where we will not know it yet. That is the whole diagram. Features on the left, label on the right, one row per example, many rows making the training data. During training, the machine sees both sides, the features and the label, so it can compare its guess with the truth and nudge its dials. Later, in real use, the machine sees only the features of a new case, and it must produce the label on its own. That difference, seeing the answer during training and not seeing it in real use, is the single most important fact in this lesson, so say it with me in plain words. In training, the machine sees the features and the label. In real use, the machine sees only the features and must guess the label. Hold onto that. Almost every mistake in this field is a way of forgetting it.

Let us fill the table with a real example from a small business, slowly, row by row. Imagine you run a tree service. Homeowners call you for quotes, and you want to predict how long a job will take, so you can price it fairly and plan your crew's day. Each past job becomes one row. What could the features be? The height of the tree, in feet, is a feature. Whether the tree is dead or alive is a feature. How close the tree stands to the house, in feet, is a feature. Whether you need a crane, yes or no, is a feature. The label is how many hours the job actually took. Notice the shape of that. The features are things you can know before the job starts, when you stand in the yard and look up. The label is the thing you only know after the job is done. That timing is no accident, and it is a test you can apply to any feature anyone proposes. Can I know this before I need the prediction? If yes, it can be a feature. If I only know it afterwards, it cannot help me predict in real use, however interesting it is. A feature must be available at prediction time. That sentence deserves its place on the board. A feature must be available at prediction time. The hours taken fail that test for the next job, which is exactly why hours taken are the label and not a feature. We want to predict them precisely because we do not have them yet.

Now a tiny worked example with numbers small enough to follow in your head, because features earn their keep only when you see them do work. Suppose your notebook holds three past jobs. Job one, a tree thirty feet tall, alive, twenty feet from the house, no crane, and the job took two hours. Job two, a tree sixty feet tall, dead, ten feet from the house, crane needed, and the job took six hours. Job three, a tree forty feet tall, alive, fifteen feet from the house, no crane, and the job took three hours. Three rows, four features each, one label each. Now a new call comes in. A tree fifty feet tall, alive, twelve feet from the house, no crane. How long might it take? Your eye, and a simple model, would reason the same way. It is taller than jobs one and three, so longer than their two and three hours. It needs no crane and is alive, unlike job two, so shorter than six hours. A guess of about four hours sits sensibly in the middle. That guess used the features and nothing else. It did not peek at the answer, because for the new job there is no answer yet. And notice which feature did the heavy lifting. Height moved the guess most, crane need moved it a lot when present, and aliveness and distance refined it. In real models, features differ in how much they matter, and part of training is the machine discovering those amounts for itself, as dial settings, from many rows. With three rows it is a hunch. With three hundred rows it becomes a tool you can price with. The structure, though, is identical at both sizes. Features in view, label to predict, rows to learn from.

Features come in kinds, and the kind decides how the machine reads them, so let us name the kinds plainly. A numeric feature is a number on a scale, like height in feet, distance in feet, temperature, or price in dollars. Numbers are the machine's favourite food, because arithmetic works on them directly. A category feature is a choice from a fixed list, like alive or dead, sunny or rainy, referral or advert or walk-in. Categories are not numbers, and treating them as if they were can mislead. If you code sunny as one, rainy as two and cloudy as three, the machine may think cloudy is three times sunny, which is nonsense that you accidentally taught it. The honest fix, which you will meet properly in later courses, is to give each category its own yes-or-no column. Sunny, yes or no. Rainy, yes or no. Cloudy, yes or no. Three honest columns instead of one dishonest number. A text feature is words, like the message a customer wrote on your contact form. Machines cannot eat raw words, so text gets counted and weighed first, how many times certain telling words appear, for example, before it can join the table. And a yes-or-no feature, like crane needed, is the simplest of all, one for yes and zero for no. You do not need to master the machinery of any of this today. You need the instinct. Every feature must end up as honest numbers that mean what they claim to mean, or the patterns the machine finds will be patterns in your coding mistakes, not in the world.

Now the shadow side, and I will spend real time here because this is where beginners, and frankly some professionals, lose the most money. The first shadow is the cheating feature, known in the field as leakage, a word worth learning properly. Leakage means information from the label, or from after the moment of prediction, has leaked into the features. The model then looks brilliant in training and collapses in real use, because in real use that leaked information will not be there. Here is a clean example. Suppose you want to predict, when a quote is requested, whether the homeowner will accept your price. One of your columns is days until the deposit was paid. For customers who accepted, that column holds a small number. For customers who refused, it is blank forever. A model trained with that column will learn the rule, if deposit days exist, the answer is yes, and it will score nearly perfectly on your old rows. It has learned nothing about customers. It has learned to read the answer off the back of the envelope. On a new quote, where nobody has paid anything yet, the column is always blank, and the model is helpless. The tell-tale sign of leakage is a model that looks too good. If your first model is right ninety-nine times out of one hundred on a fuzzy human question, do not celebrate. Suspect leakage, and go hunting for the feature that already knows the answer. Perfect scores on fuzzy problems are not a triumph. They are an alarm bell. Write that down exactly as I said it. Perfect scores on fuzzy problems are an alarm bell.

The second shadow is the missing feature, the clue you never gave the machine. A model can only use the features in its table. If the real driver of the label is not among them, no amount of training will invent it. Imagine predicting which website visitors become clients, using only the colour scheme of the page they landed on and the hour of the day, while never recording how they found you or whether they opened your follow-up email. The model will squeeze those two weak features dry and still guess poorly, and the poor result will not mean machine learning failed. It will mean the table was starved. The fix is not a fancier model. The fix is better features, chosen by someone who understands the real business. This is why the person who knows the work matters so much in machine learning. Choosing features is where human knowledge enters the table. A tree surgeon knows that lean, rot and power lines matter before any data scientist does. A marketer knows that referral source matters. The machine finds the pattern, but you choose what it is allowed to look at, and that choice is a skilled, human, billable act. Never let anyone tell you the machine does it all. The table is yours. The features are your expertise, written down in columns.

The third shadow is quieter. A feature can be present, honest, available in time, and still be unfair or unlawful to use, and a professional has to catch that before training, not after a complaint. If your table includes a feature that stands in for a protected characteristic of a person, the model's rules may quietly discriminate even if you never intended them to. The lesson for today is simple and firm. Features are choices, and choices carry responsibility. Ask of every column not only does it help, and is it available in time, but also should it be used at all. That question belongs to the human at the table, and no dial setting can answer it for you. I raise it now, early in your education, so it becomes a habit while your habits are forming, not a patch you bolt on later.

Let me give you a second worked example, from marketing this time, with the label as a yes-or-no answer, because labels are not always numbers. A number label, like hours or jars sold, is called a regression label in the field, from an old statistical word, and a yes-or-no or category label, like became a client or did not, is called a classification label, because the model is sorting cases into classes. You do not need to love those terms, but you will hear them, so now they are unpacked. Your form records two hundred people. For each person, the features are these. How they found you, referral, advert or search. The size of their business, as a number of staff. Whether they opened the follow-up email, yes or no. The label is whether they became a paying client within a month, yes or no. Let us count together, tiny numbers again. Of the two hundred people, fifty came by referral, and thirty of those fifty became clients. Thirty out of fifty is sixty percent, a strong rate. One hundred came by advert, and only ten of those became clients. Ten out of one hundred is ten percent. Already, with one feature alone, the table is speaking. Referral predicts far better than advert. Now add the email feature inside the referral group. Of the fifty referrals, forty opened the email, and twenty-eight of those forty became clients. Twenty-eight out of forty is seventy percent. The ten referrals who never opened it produced only two clients, twenty percent. Each honest feature sharpens the picture a little more. That sharpening, done systematically over all the features at once, is exactly what training automates. You are not learning a new kind of thinking today. You are learning to see the thinking you already do with counts and rates, laid out as a table the machine can work on at scale.

Time for our guided think-it moment. Take the tree service table in your mind and test three proposed new columns. Column A, the customer's star rating of your company after the job. Column B, whether power lines run through the tree's branches, noted at quote time. Column C, the final invoice total. For each column, ask the two questions from this lesson. Can I know it before I need the prediction? And does it secretly contain the answer? Take a breath and judge them one by one. Here are my judgments. Column A fails. A rating given after the job is not available when you price the job, and worse, a happy rating leaks the fact that the job went well. Column B passes cleanly. Power lines are visible at quote time, they genuinely make work slower, and they contain no hint of the label. That is a fine feature, and a tree surgeon's knowledge put it there, not a computer's. Column C fails twice over. The invoice is written after the job, and since you price by hours, the invoice is practically the label wearing a coat. Using it would be leakage in its purest form. If you judged B as the only keeper, you have the instinct this lesson exists to build. Guard it. It will save you from the most common and most embarrassing failure in applied machine learning.

One more practical piece before we recap, and it is about scale, a small thing that bites hard. Features live on different scales. Height in feet runs from ten to one hundred. Crane needed runs from zero to one. Distance in feet runs from five to fifty. If you feed those raw numbers to some models, the big-numbered feature shouts and the small-numbered feature whispers, even when the whisper matters more. The common fix is to rescale features so they sit on comparable footing, for example squeezing each one into a range from zero to one. You will do this properly in later work. Today, just file the idea. Numbers that look bigger are not automatically more important, and honest modelling makes sure the machine is not fooled by the size of the units somebody happened to measure in. Feet versus metres should never change what a model concludes about a tree, and rescaling is how we keep that promise.

Let me walk one complete table past you from a different trade, so the structure proves it is not about trees. Imagine a small bakery deciding how many loaves to bake each morning, the same bakery shape you met last lesson, now with its table drawn properly. Each past morning is a row. The features are the day of the week, whether school is in, whether roadworks are active on the main road, and the forecast, sunny or rainy. Four features, two of them categories, one of them yes-or-no, one of them a day name. The label is the number of loaves sold by ten o'clock. Now say the sentence that must always be sayable. In training, the baker's notebook shows the machine the features and the label together, sixty mornings of them. In real use, tomorrow morning, the baker knows the day, the school calendar, the roadworks and the forecast, all features, all available before the ovens are lit, and the machine must guess the label, loaves sold, which nobody knows until ten o'clock arrives. If a proposed fifth feature appears, say the length of the queue at nine o'clock, you already know how to judge it. It sounds predictive, and it is, but at baking time, hours before nine, it does not exist yet. It fails the availability test, and including it would train a model the baker can never actually use at the moment of decision. Timing is not a detail in this work. Timing is the difference between a model that helps at the moment of decision and a model that only explains yesterday beautifully. Businesses do not need beautiful explanations of yesterday nearly as much as they need decent guesses before today is spent.

While we are here, let me settle a confusion about labels that I hear every year, because clearing it now saves real pain. The label must be defined exactly, in words a stranger could apply the same way you do. Became a client sounds clear until you ask, within what time, a week, a month, a year, and paid how much, anything at all, or a full package? Job took long sounds clear until you ask whether travel and waiting for a crane count in the hours. Every vague label teaches the machine a vague target, and the machine will hit that vague target with great precision and no usefulness. Professionals write the label definition down before training starts, in one sentence, and they defend that sentence like a contract. Ours for the tree service was, hours from arrival on site to departure, including waiting time on site. Ours for the marketing table was, paid at least one full invoice within thirty days of the form. Notice how each definition settles arguments before they start. If two people labelling the same cases would often disagree, the label is not ready, and no model built on it can be trusted, however impressive its score looks. Clean labels are quiet, unglamorous, decisive work. They are also, hour for hour, some of the highest-value work in the entire field, because every dial downstream learns from them.

And one word about having too many features, since beginners often assume more columns must mean more learning. More features can help when each one adds a genuinely new clue. But every added column is also another chance for leakage to sneak in, another column to collect reliably forever, and another way for the model to find a fluke pattern in a small table that will not repeat in the world. With two hundred rows and three hundred features, a model can practically memorise, a sin we will dissect properly in lesson five under its name, overfitting. The craft is not collecting the most features. The craft is choosing a lean set of honest, available, meaningful features and defending each one's place in the table. If you cannot say, in one plain sentence, why a feature might genuinely relate to the label, that feature is a guest you have not vetted. Vetting guests is the job. A short table you understand beats a wide table you merely hope in, every single time, in every trade I have ever seen this applied to.

Let me do one more slow count together, because reading a table fluently is a skill and skills grow by doing. Back to the tree service, with a fresh little notebook of four jobs where the only feature we will track is whether a crane was needed, and the label is hours taken. Job one, no crane, two hours. Job two, no crane, three hours. Job three, crane needed, six hours. Job four, crane needed, seven hours. Four rows. Now squeeze the table the way your eye already wants to. The no-crane jobs average two and a half hours, because two and three average to two and a half. The crane jobs average six and a half hours, because six and seven average to six and a half. The gap between the groups is four hours. That gap is the feature earning its keep in plain sight. If a fifth job arrives needing a crane, your table-trained guess starts near six and a half hours, then refines with height and distance when those columns join. If a job arrives with no crane, you start near two and a half. One honest feature has already sorted the future into two sensible piles. That is all a model ever does, however large it grows. It sorts the future into sensible piles using the features, weighted by what the labelled past says each feature is worth. When someone shows you a model you cannot interrogate, bring it back to this. Show me the table. Show me the features. Show me the label definition. Show me a count like the one we just did, where one feature visibly moves the label. If the table cannot be shown, the magic is probably bookkeeping. You now own the questions that separate the two, and you learned them from four tree jobs and a bakery. That is how foundations are supposed to work.

One final habit to install before the recap, and then we really will recap. Whenever you meet a new dataset, read it column by column and say each column's job out loud. Feature, feature, feature, label. Then read it row by row and ask whether the row is honest, complete enough to learn from, and labelled by the definition you wrote down. Column by column for jobs, row by row for honesty. That two-direction reading takes ten minutes on a small table and catches leakage, starved features, vague labels and miscoded categories while they are still cheap to fix. Every expensive failure I have watched in this field was visible in that ten-minute reading to anyone willing to do it slowly. Slow reading is not the opposite of progress here. Slow reading is what makes the fast machinery safe to trust.

Recap, in order, as always. First, every example is a row, features on the left, label on the right. Features are the clues the machine is shown, and the label is the correct answer it must learn to predict. Second, in training the machine sees features and label together, but in real use it sees only the features, so every feature must be available at prediction time. Third, features come in kinds, numeric, category, text, and yes-or-no, and each kind must be turned into honest numbers that mean what they claim to mean. Fourth, leakage is the cheating shadow, answer information hiding in the features, and its warning sign is a score that looks too perfect on a fuzzy problem. Fifth, missing features starve the table, and choosing features is where human expertise enters, which makes it skilled and responsible work. Sixth, number labels and category labels lead to the two great families of task, predicting an amount and sorting into classes, and you have now seen honest counts for both.

Carry one sentence out of the room with you and the lesson has done its work even if details fade. The machine can only learn from what it is shown, so showing it well, honest features on the left and an exactly defined label on the right, is not preparation for the real work. It is the real work, and everything clever that follows stands on it.

That closes lesson two. You can now look at any proposed machine learning project and ask the questions that matter. What is the label, exactly? What are the features, exactly? Can each feature be known in time, and does any of them already know the answer? Those questions will expose most bad projects in five minutes flat. In our next lesson, The loss function, a number that says wrong, this much, we will give the machine its sense of wrongness. We will ask, when a guess misses, how do we turn that miss into a single honest number the dials can learn from, and why the choice of that number changes what the machine bothers to get right. The questions for this lesson are ready now, built only from what I taught here, and the full text stays open beside them. Reading back is learning, not cheating, so go back as often as you like. And remember, if sorting features from labels feels tangled at first, stuck is a place, not a person. You are just passing through it. I will see you in lesson three.

lessons.title: The loss function: a number that says 'wrong, this much'
paragraphs: Welcome back, in, in. I am Professor Sana Rahal, and this is Machine Learning One, lesson three, The loss function, a number that says wrong, this much. In lesson one we met the four beats of training. Guess, compare, nudge, repeat. In lesson two we opened the example and separated the features, the clues, from the label, the correct answer. Today we stay on the second beat, compare, and we give it the respect it deserves, because compare sounds simple until you ask the obvious question. Compare how? When the model's guess misses the truth, how wrong is it, exactly, and how do we turn that wrongness into one honest number that the dials can learn from? That number has a name. It is called the loss, and the recipe that produces it is called the loss function. A loss function is a rule that takes a guess and the true label and returns a single number measuring how bad the guess was. Zero loss means a perfect guess. Bigger loss means a worse guess. By the end of this lesson you will be able to calculate a simple loss by hand, explain why we often square the error instead of just measuring it plainly, say what average loss over many examples tells us, and understand why choosing a loss function is really choosing what the machine will care about. That last idea is deeper than it looks, so stay with me all the way to the end.

Let us draw today's diagram before naming anything else, in the usual way. Picture a guess on the left and the truth on the right, with a gap between them. Underneath, a funnel. Both the guess and the truth drop into the funnel, the funnel does arithmetic, and out of the bottom comes one number. That number is the loss. Everything in training hangs off that number. If the loss is high, the nudges to the dials are urgent. If the loss is low, the nudges are gentle. If the loss is zero, there is nothing to fix on that example. The loss is the machine's sense of wrongness, its only sense of wrongness, in fact. A model does not feel embarrassment or pride. It feels, if we can use that word loosely, exactly what the loss function tells it to feel. Choose a bad loss function and you have built a machine that cares about the wrong thing, diligently, at great speed. Choose a good one and the same machinery cares about what you care about. That is why this modest little funnel gets a whole lesson to itself.

Start with the simplest honest measure. The model guesses a number, the truth is a number, and we subtract. The difference is called the error. If the truth is twenty-one jars and the guess is eighteen jars, the error is three jars, because twenty-one minus eighteen is three. Plain, clear, and already useful, but with one flaw we must fix immediately. Errors can be negative. If the guess is twenty-four and the truth is twenty-one, the subtraction the other way gives minus three, and if we average a plus three error with a minus three error we get zero, which would claim the model is perfect when it missed twice, once low and once high. A loss that can cancel its own mistakes is a liar. So we must make every error positive before we combine them. There are two classic ways to do that, and the difference between them shapes everything, so we will take them one at a time and calculate both with our bare hands.

The first way is the absolute error. Absolute is a word from ordinary mathematics that here just means ignore the sign, treat minus three as three. The absolute error is simply how far the guess is from the truth, ignoring direction. Guess eighteen, truth twenty-one, absolute error three. Guess twenty-four, truth twenty-one, absolute error also three. Both misses hurt equally, by three jars. If we average the absolute errors over all our examples, we get a number called the mean absolute error, where mean is just the ordinary word for average. Mean absolute error is beautifully understandable, because it speaks in the original units. A mean absolute error of three jars means, on average, our guesses are three jars away from the truth. A business owner can hold that number in her head and decide if it is good enough to bake by. Keep it in mind as the honest, plain-spoken option. We will meet its rival now, and the rival wins more often in practice, for a reason you can feel with tiny numbers.

The second way is the squared error. Squared means multiplied by itself. Instead of ignoring the sign, we square the error, and squaring makes everything positive automatically, because minus three times minus three is plus nine, and plus three times plus three is also nine. Guess eighteen, truth twenty-one, error three, squared error nine. Guess twenty-four, truth twenty-one, error minus three, squared error also nine. So far the two methods agree in spirit. The difference appears when errors grow. Watch carefully, with small numbers first. An error of one squares to one. An error of two squares to four. An error of three squares to nine. An error of ten squares to one hundred. Do you see the pattern? Squaring does not just measure the miss, it punishes big misses far more than small ones. Being wrong by ten costs not ten times an error of one, but one hundred times. Averaging squared errors over all examples gives the mean squared error, the most common loss in the kind of number-predicting work we have been doing. And that punishment of big misses is usually exactly what we want. Think about the bakery. Guessing eighteen when the truth is twenty-one wastes a little. Guessing five when the truth is twenty-one means turning away a queue of customers and losing a morning's reputation. The second failure is much worse than three times the first, and squared error knows it, while absolute error treats every jar as equal. The loss function is where we tell the machine how much worse big failures are. It is a values statement written in arithmetic.

Let us calculate a full tiny example together, every step spoken, so the funnel stops being a picture and becomes a skill. Our jam model makes guesses for three Saturdays, and we know the truths from the notebook. Saturday one, guess twenty, truth twenty-one. The error is one, because twenty-one minus twenty is one. Squared error is one times one, which is one. Saturday two, guess eighteen, truth twenty-two. The error is four, because twenty-two minus eighteen is four. Squared error is four times four, which is sixteen. Saturday three, guess twelve, truth eleven. The error is minus one, or one in size, because the guess is one too high. Squared error is one. Now average the three squared errors. One plus sixteen plus one is eighteen. Eighteen divided by three is six. So the mean squared error is six. Say the whole story back in words. Three guesses, squared errors of one, sixteen and one, mean squared error six. Notice which Saturday dominates the loss. Saturday two, with its error of four, contributed sixteen of the eighteen total. That is squaring doing its job in public, pointing the training process at the worst miss and saying, fix that one first, it is where the pain is. If we had used absolute errors instead, the three errors would be one, four and one, averaging to two, a mean absolute error of two jars. Both summaries are honest. They emphasise different things. Two jars average miss is the plain report for the owner. Six, the mean squared error, is the sharper training signal for the dials. Professionals often train with one and report with the other, and now you know why both exist.

There is a third member of the family you will hear named, so let us unpack it briefly and move on. Take the mean squared error and take its square root, the number which multiplied by itself gives it back. That is called the root mean squared error. Its virtue is that it speaks in the original units again, jars rather than jars squared, while keeping the big-miss punishment of squaring. If the mean squared error is six, the root is a little under two and a half, since two and a half times two and a half is six and a quarter. Close enough for a head calculation, and I show it so the term never intimidates you. You now own the whole little family. Error, the signed gap. Absolute error, the gap ignoring sign. Squared error, the gap multiplied by itself. Mean squared error, the average of squared errors, and its root, back in honest units. Five phrases, all built from one subtraction. That is most of what the phrase loss function ever means in number prediction, and it was arithmetic you could already do.

Now, what about labels that are not numbers, the classification world from lesson two, where the label is yes or no, client or not client, junk or not junk? The funnel still works, but the arithmetic inside it changes shape. The model does not guess yes outright. It guesses a confidence, a number between zero and one, like zero point nine for almost certainly yes, or zero point two for probably not. The loss then punishes confident wrongness savagely and shrugs at humble wrongness. If the truth is yes and the model said zero point nine, the loss is small. If the truth is yes and the model said zero point one, confidently wrong, the loss is large. The exact recipe has a name you will meet in later courses, and I am deliberately not loading you with it today, because the principle matters more than the formula at this stage. The principle is identical across both worlds. Loss is one number that says wrong, this much, and confident, large wrongness always costs more than small, uncertain wrongness. A model trained under such a loss learns not just to guess, but to know how sure it should be, which in business is often the difference between a useful tool and a dangerous one. A score of zero point five one is a coin flip wearing a suit. A score of zero point nine five is a claim. The loss function is what teaches the machine the difference between those two voices.

Here is where the lesson turns from arithmetic to judgment, and I think it is the most important turn in the whole course so far. The loss function only counts what you put in it. If your loss counts jars missed, the machine will optimise jars missed, and it will cheerfully sacrifice things you forgot to count. Imagine training the bakery model on loss measured only in unsold loaves wasted, never counting customers turned away empty-handed. The machine will discover the safest strategy of all, bake very little, waste almost nothing, and send half the street away hungry. Its loss will look wonderful. Its business will rot. The machine did exactly what the loss told it to do. The failure was in the funnel, not the dials. Professionals therefore ask, before any training, what does the loss leave out, and who pays for what it leaves out? In medicine the asymmetry is stark. Missing a real illness and falsely alarming a healthy person are both errors, but they are not equal errors, and honest loss functions weight them differently on purpose. In quoting tree work, overestimating hours loses you the job, underestimating loses you money on the day, and a good loss knows those costs differ. Choosing the loss function is choosing the machine's conscience. It is human, ethical, commercial judgment, expressed as arithmetic, and it cannot be delegated to the machine itself, because the machine's whole job is to serve that number. Whoever writes the loss writes the values. Remember that sentence when vendors wave scores at you. Always ask, wrong according to which loss, counted in what units, leaving out what costs?

Our guided think-it moment today is a calculation and a judgment together, the way real work always mixes them. Your delivery driver model predicts arrival times for three deliveries, in minutes from now. It guesses ten, twenty and thirty minutes. The true arrivals are twelve, twenty and forty minutes. First, calculate with me. Delivery one, error two, squared error four. Delivery two, error zero, squared error zero, a perfect guess. Delivery three, error ten, squared error one hundred. Total squared error, four plus zero plus one hundred, is one hundred and four. Divide by three and the mean squared error is about thirty-four point seven, though the exact decimal matters less than what you notice. One delivery, the third, contributes one hundred of the one hundred and four. Now the judgment. If you reported only the mean absolute error, which is two plus zero plus ten, divided by three, which is four minutes, your report would sound calm. Four minutes average miss. But a customer waited ten extra minutes once in three deliveries, and that one wait is the story your reputation will tell. Which number do you show the owner, and which do you train on? My answer, train on the squared loss so the dials chase the big miss, and report both numbers to the owner, the calm average and the worst miss, because owners deserve the whole truth in units they understand. If your thinking ran that way, calculation plus judgment together, you are already thinking like a practitioner and not a button-pusher.

Two cautions to finish the teaching, both small and both able to sink a project. First, loss is measured on examples, and it can be gamed by the examples you choose. Measure loss only on easy cases and it will flatter you. Measure it on the same cases you trained on and it will flatter you again, for a deeper reason that lesson five and lesson six will expose fully. The loss number is only as honest as the cases it was measured on. Second, lower loss is better, always, but loss can never go below the noise in the world itself. Some Saturdays, a road closes, a school trip appears, and no model using your features could have known. That irreducible surprise puts a floor under your loss, and chasing loss below that floor means fitting noise, which is overfitting arriving early to say hello. A wise practitioner expects a floor, respects it, and gets suspicious of any loss suspiciously beneath it. Perfection is not the goal of this funnel. Honest, useful wrongness, shrinking steadily, is the goal.

Let me add one more concrete business pass, because loss functions become real when money attaches to them. Suppose your marketing model scores leads and you act on scores above a line, calling those people first. Every call costs you twenty minutes. Every missed future client costs you a job worth real money. A loss that counts only wrong classifications, treating a missed client and a wasted call as equal, will tune the machine to a balance point that suits nobody. Weight the missed client five times the wasted call, inside the loss, and the machine shifts, flagging more people as promising, wasting some calls, missing fewer clients. Nothing about the data changed. Nothing about the model shape changed. Only the loss changed, and the behaviour followed. That experiment, which you can now describe to any business owner in plain words, proves the lesson's thesis better than any definition. The loss function is the steering wheel. The model is only the engine. People argue about engines because engines are shiny. Professionals argue about steering, because steering decides where you arrive.

Before the recap, let me show you the loss doing its daily work inside training, one full round of the four beats with real numbers, so lessons one and three lock together. Take the sunny-day jam dial from lesson one. The dial currently says sixteen jars for a sunny day. A sunny example arrives with a true label of twenty jars. Beat one, guess, sixteen. Beat two, compare, and now compare has machinery. The error is four, the squared loss is sixteen. That sixteen is not just a report, it is an instruction with a size. A loss of sixteen says this dial is meaningfully low, nudge it upward by a noticeable amount, not a whisper. The dial moves to eighteen. Next sunny example, truth twenty-one. Guess eighteen, error three, squared loss nine. Smaller loss, smaller nudge, dial to nineteen and a half, let us say. Next, truth twenty. Guess nineteen and a half, error a half, squared loss a quarter. Tiny loss, tiny nudge. Watch the rhythm across the three rounds. Sixteen, nine, a quarter. The loss is falling as the dial homes in, and the size of each nudge follows the size of the loss. That coupling, big loss big nudge, small loss small nudge, is what makes training settle instead of bouncing forever around the answer. In lesson four we will make the direction of the nudge just as principled as its size, but even now you can see the whole engine's heartbeat. The loss number is both the speedometer and, in embryo, the steering signal. When people say a model is training, this rhythm, guess, loss, nudge, guess, loss, nudge, thousands or millions of times, is literally what is happening inside the machine, and there is no additional mystery hidden behind it.

Let me also protect you from a word trick you will meet in the wild, because this class believes in naming fog when we see it. People sometimes report accuracy instead of loss, saying the model is ninety percent accurate. Accuracy is the share of guesses counted as right, and for classification it can be a fair summary, but it hides everything this lesson taught you to ask. Ninety percent accurate at what cost for the ten percent? Were the wrong ones confident or humble, cheap or ruinous? A model that is ninety percent accurate while being confidently wrong about every serious illness is a bad model wearing a good number. Loss, honestly chosen and honestly reported in units the owner understands, cannot hide those sins as easily, because the big misses swell it visibly. So your professional habit from today onward is this. Whenever a score is waved at you, translate it. What was counted, what was left out, in what units, and on which cases was it measured? Four questions, and the fog either clears or the vendor does. Either outcome is information you earned with arithmetic a child could check. That is not a small power. Most of the money wasted in this field is wasted by people who never learned to ask what the number leaves out, and you learned it in lesson three, with jam, deliveries and loaves.

One more distinction, small in words and large in consequences, and then the recap will gather everything. Loss is calculated per example first, one funnel, one guess, one truth, one number. Only afterwards do we average across examples to get the summary the training follows. That order matters because averages can hide a disaster in one corner of your data. A model can post a lovely low average loss while failing every single customer from one neighbourhood, one age group, or one kind of tree, if those cases are few among many. The average is calm. The corner is burning. Practitioners therefore slice the loss, calculating it separately for meaningful groups, and look at the worst slice, not just the mean. If the worst slice is far worse than the average, the model has a blind spot with an address, and fixing it usually means more or better examples from that corner, not more training on the whole pile. You will not be asked to run sliced audits in this course, but you will be expected, from now on, to hear an average and immediately wonder about the corners it might be hiding. Averages summarise. Corners confess. A good analyst listens to both.

And since we are building habits, here is the habit for checking any loss calculation you are handed, in thirty seconds, with no tools. First, pick one example and recompute its loss yourself from the guess and the truth. One funnel, by hand. If that one does not match, nothing downstream can be trusted. Second, find the largest single loss in the set and ask whether it deserves to dominate. If the biggest loss comes from a mislabelled example, a typo in the notebook, a truth that was recorded wrong, then the loudest voice in your training is a clerical error, and the dials will chase a ghost. Label errors shout under squared loss precisely because squaring amplifies whatever is biggest, wisdom or garbage alike. Third, ask what a loss of zero would require, and whether the world, with its road closures and surprises, would ever allow it. If zero is impossible, say what floor you expect and why. Those three checks, recompute one, interrogate the biggest, name the floor, will catch most loss nonsense before it costs anyone money. They are yours now, permanently, and they work on every loss function you will ever meet, including the ones with intimidating names in later courses, because underneath every one of them sits the same funnel, a guess, a truth, and a number that says wrong, this much.

Recap, in order. First, the loss is a single number that says how wrong a guess was, produced by a recipe called the loss function, and zero loss means a perfect guess. Second, the error is guess versus truth, and because signed errors cancel dishonestly, we make them positive, by absolute value or by squaring. Third, squared error punishes big misses far more than small ones, an error of ten costing one hundred, and the mean squared error averages that punishment across examples. Fourth, in our worked example the squared errors were one, sixteen and one, giving a mean squared error of six, dominated by the worst miss, exactly as intended. Fifth, classification has its own loss shape, punishing confident wrongness most, so models learn how sure to be, not just what to guess. Sixth, and above all, the loss only counts what you put in it, so choosing the loss function is choosing what the machine cares about, and whoever writes the loss writes the values.

Try one last pair of numbers in your head before you go, just to feel the funnel in your fingers. Guess thirty, truth twenty-five. Error five, absolute error five, squared error twenty-five. Now guess twenty-six, truth twenty-five. Error one, squared error one. The second guess is five times closer in plain distance, but twenty-five times better in squared loss. That magnification of improvement near the truth is why squared loss pulls dials so eagerly toward good guesses, and why the final small improvements in training, from good to very good, register so clearly in the number even when the eye can barely see them in the guesses themselves.

You did the arithmetic today, slowly, honestly, and completely, checking each step against the truth the way a loss function itself would want to be checked, without flattery and without fear of the answer, all of it, in your head, with jars and minutes and loaves. Never let anyone convince you this subject floats above you. It stands exactly where you are standing.

Carry this out of the room. Every impressive score you will ever be shown is a loss function in disguise, wearing its Sunday clothes. Ask what it counts, ask what it leaves out, ask on which cases it was measured, and you will see the machine's actual values standing behind the number, every time.

That closes lesson three. You can now take any guess and any truth, run them through the funnel yourself, and say wrong, this much, in a number you calculated and can defend. You also know the question that cuts through sales talk. Wrong according to which loss? In our next lesson, Gradient descent, walking downhill in the dark, we follow that number downhill. We will ask how the machine, knowing only how wrong it currently is, can figure out which way to nudge thousands of dials so the loss falls, step by step, without ever seeing the whole landscape. It is the cleverest idea in the course, and it is built entirely on the number you learned today. The questions for this lesson are waiting, built only from what I taught, with the full text open beside them. Calculating along with the text is learning, not cheating. Take your time, keep your arithmetic in words if that helps, and remember the door sign. Stuck is a place, not a person, and today you walked straight through the place most beginners fear, the maths, and found it was only subtraction, multiplication and honest judgment. I will see you in lesson four.

questions.q: What do we call the single number that measures how bad a guess was?
questions.teach: From the lesson: Zero loss means a perfect guess and a bigger loss means a worse guess.
questions.teach2: "That number has a name. It is called the loss, and the recipe that produces it is called the loss function." Zero loss means a perfect guess and a bigger loss means a worse guess.
questions.walk: Walk it through step by step: (1) A guess and the truth go into the funnel. (2) One number comes out measuring wrongness. (3) That number is called the loss, so the answer is loss.

questions.q: What do we call the recipe that takes a guess and the true label and returns a number measuring how bad the guess was?
questions.teach: From the lesson: Every training nudge depends on the number this recipe produces.
questions.teach2: "A loss function is a rule that takes a guess and the true label and returns a single number measuring how bad the guess was." Every training nudge depends on the number this recipe produces.
questions.walk: Walk it through step by step: (1) The funnel takes a guess and the truth. (2) It does arithmetic and returns one number. (3) The recipe inside the funnel is the loss function.

questions.q: What does a loss of zero mean?
questions.teach: From the lesson: When the guess matches the truth exactly there is nothing to fix on that example.
questions.teach2: "Zero loss means a perfect guess. Bigger loss means a worse guess." When the guess matches the truth exactly there is nothing to fix on that example.
questions.walk: Walk it through step by step: (1) Loss measures how bad a guess was. (2) The smallest possible value is zero. (3) Zero happens only when the guess is perfect, so the answer is a perfect guess.

questions.q: The truth is twenty-one jars and the model guesses eighteen jars. What is the size of the error, in words?
questions.teach: From the lesson: Subtracting the guess from the truth gives the error size.
questions.teach2: "If the truth is twenty-one jars and the guess is eighteen jars, the error is three jars, because twenty-one minus eighteen is three." Subtracting the guess from the truth gives the error size.
questions.walk: Walk it through step by step: (1) Subtract eighteen from twenty-one. (2) Twenty-one minus eighteen is three. (3) So the answer is three.

questions.q: An error of three is squared to punish it. What is the squared error, in words?
questions.teach: From the lesson: Squaring means multiplying the error by itself, so three becomes nine.
questions.teach2: "Guess eighteen, truth twenty-one, error three, squared error nine." Squaring means multiplying the error by itself, so three becomes nine.
questions.walk: Walk it through step by step: (1) The error is three. (2) Multiply three by three. (3) That gives nine, so the answer is nine.

questions.q: What does an error of ten become when it is squared, in words?
questions.teach: From the lesson: That is why squaring punishes a big miss far more than a small one.
questions.teach2: "An error of one squares to one. An error of two squares to four. An error of three squares to nine. An error of ten squares to one hundred." That is why squaring punishes a big miss far more than a small one.
questions.walk: Walk it through step by step: (1) The error is ten. (2) Multiply ten by ten. (3) That gives one hundred, so the answer is one hundred.

questions.q: Which kind of error punishes big misses far more than small ones, so an error of ten costs one hundred times an error of one?
questions.teach: From the lesson: An error of one costs one while an error of ten costs one hundred under this method.
questions.teach2: "Squaring does not just measure the miss, it punishes big misses far more than small ones." An error of one costs one while an error of ten costs one hundred under this method.
questions.walk: Walk it through step by step: (1) One squared is one and ten squared is one hundred. (2) The cost grows much faster than the miss. (3) That method is squared error, so the answer is squared error.

questions.q: Three guesses have squared errors of one, sixteen and one. What is the mean squared error, in words?
questions.teach: From the lesson: Averaging the three squared errors gives the training summary from the worked example.

questions.walk: Walk it through step by step: (1) Add one, sixteen and one to get eighteen. (2) Divide eighteen by three examples. (3) That gives six, so the answer is six.

questions.teach: From the lesson: Absolute errors ignore the sign and average in the original units.
